result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Survey Design and Weights" subtitle: "Strata · PSUs · selection probabilities · sampling weights · declaring the design · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Earlier workshops: data from a **simple random sample** (every person equally likely, independent) - Today: **household surveys** (NFHS, NCD risk-factor surveys, district surveys) do **not** work that way - By the end you can: - name the three features that make survey data different - explain what a **sampling weight** is - see why **unweighted** estimates are biased - **declare the design** in R with `svydesign()` ::: ## What is different about survey data | Feature | Why it is used | Effect on analysis | |---|---|---| | **Stratification** | guarantee a sample in every region and in urban and rural areas | variance is **smaller** (strata are separated) | | **Clustering** (PSUs) | visit a few villages or census blocks, not people scattered everywhere | variance is **larger** (people in a PSU are alike) | | **Unequal probabilities** | oversample small or important groups | estimates are **biased unless weighted** | ::: {.key} A **simple random sample** analysis (`mean()`, `lm()`, `t.test()`) ignores all three: the **estimate** can be biased and the **standard error** is usually **too small**. ::: ## Our survey: an adult health survey (synthetic) ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **8 strata**: 4 regions × urban/rural - **6 PSUs** per stratum (villages or blocks), chosen with probability proportional to size; then **40 to 60 adults** per PSU - **2,504 adults** sampled, **1,853** responded - **Urban areas are over-sampled**: 50% of the sample but about **28%** of the adults - Outcomes: hypertension (SBP ≥ 140), diabetes, SBP, BMI ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resp |> select(stratum, psu, weight, age, sex, residence, sbp, hypertension) |> head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 stratum psu weight age sex residence sbp hypertension 1 North Urban NU16 132. 65 Female Urban 147 1 2 North Urban NU16 157. 46 Female Urban 142 1 3 North Urban NU16 165. 50 Male Urban 139 0 4 North Urban NU16 161. 38 Male Urban 140 1 5 North Urban NU16 161. 41 Male Urban 139 0 6 North Urban NU16 161. 35 Male Urban 122 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Weights {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## What is a sampling weight? ::: {.eq} weight = 1 / (probability of being selected) ::: ::: {.incremental} - A respondent with weight **200** was one of about **1 in 200** adults who could have been chosen: he or she **represents about 200 adults** - Over-sampled groups have **small** weights; under-sampled groups have **large** weights - Weights are also **adjusted for nonresponse** (Session 4) - The **sum of the weights** estimates the **population size** ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(respondents = nrow(resp), sum_of_weights = round(sum(resp$weight))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` respondents sum_of_weights 1853 414476 ``` ::: ::: ## Weighted and unweighted prevalence ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(unweighted = mean(resp$hypertension), weighted = weighted.mean(resp$hypertension, resp$weight)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unweighted weighted 0.233 0.200 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} **Unweighted: 23.3%. Weighted: 20.0%.** Urban adults have more hypertension and are **over-sampled** (50% of the sample), so the raw sample over-states it. The weighted estimate **restores the population mix** (28% urban). ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rbind(sample = prop.table(table(resp$residence)), weighted = prop.table(xtabs(weight ~ residence, resp))) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rural Urban sample 0.523 0.477 weighted 0.718 0.282 ``` ::: ::: # Topic 2 — The design in R {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Declaring the design ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} des <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~weight, data = resp, nest = TRUE) des ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement) With (48) clusters. svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~weight, data = resp, nest = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - `ids`: the **primary sampling units** (PSUs); `strata`; `weights` - `nest = TRUE`: PSU labels need only be unique **within** a stratum - Declare it **once**, then use `svy*` functions for **everything** - Add `fpc =` only when a large part of the PSUs was sampled (more than about 5%) ::: ## Design-based estimate and standard error ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svymean(~hypertension, des) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean SE hypertension 0.19955 0.0149 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} p <- mean(resp$hypertension); sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nrow(resp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.009822585 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The design-based SE is **0.015**. The naive SE (simple random sample) is **0.0098**, about **one third too small**: respondents from the same PSU are alike, so there is less independent information than the sample size suggests. ::: ## Checklist when you get a survey file ::: {.good} 1. Which variables are the **strata**, **PSU** and **weight**? (read the user guide) 2. Which weight for which analysis? (household, women's, men's: **different weights**) 3. Declare the design **before** any estimate 4. Look at the **weights**: range, very large values 5. Report **unweighted n** and **weighted estimates** ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `survey-workshop/labs/lab1_design.R` - response rate, strata and PSUs - unweighted and weighted prevalence - declare the design, sum of the weights, naive vs design SE ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="6cvlyy.vyt652" data-show="SXQgaXMgdG9vIGhpZ2gsIGJlY2F1c2UgdXJiYW4gYWR1bHRzIGFyZSBvdmVyLXJlcHJlc2Vu dGVk" data-explain="T3Zlci1zYW1wbGVkIGdyb3VwcyBjb3VudCBtb3JlIGluIHRoZSByYXcgc2FtcGxlIHRoYW4g aW4gdGhlIHBvcHVsYXRpb24uIFdlaWdodHMsIHRoZSBpbnZlcnNlIG9mIHRoZSBzZWxlY3Rp b24gcHJvYmFiaWxpdGllcywgcmVzdG9yZSB0aGUgcG9wdWxhdGlvbiBtaXgu"} A survey over-samples urban adults, who have more hypertension. What happens to the unweighted prevalence? - It is too low, because urban adults get larger weights than rural ones - It is too high, because urban adults are over-represented - It is unbiased, because the sample is large enough to include every stratum - It is unbiased, but its standard error is too small to be useful ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="6cvz7p.vytkmh" data-show="VGhlIHJlc3BvbmRlbnQgc3RhbmRzIGZvciBhYm91dCAyMDAgYWR1bHRzIGluIHRoZSBwb3B1 bGF0aW9u" data-explain="VGhlIHdlaWdodCBpcyB0aGUgaW52ZXJzZSBvZiB0aGUgc2VsZWN0aW9uIHByb2JhYmlsaXR5 LCBzbyBpdCBpcyB0aGUgbnVtYmVyIG9mIGFkdWx0cyBpbiB0aGUgcG9wdWxhdGlvbiB0aGF0 IHRoZSByZXNwb25kZW50IHJlcHJlc2VudHMu"} What does a sampling weight of 200 tell you? - The respondent answered 200 questions during the household interview - The respondent comes from a PSU in which 200 adults were sampled - The answers of this respondent are 200 times more reliable than usual - The respondent stands for about 200 adults in the population ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="6cwcgb.vytz3r" data-show="QWR1bHRzIGluIHRoZSBzYW1lIFBTVSBhcmUgYWxpa2UsIGFuZCB0aGUgc3RhbmRhcmQgZXJy b3IgaGFzIHRvIHJlZmxlY3QgdGhhdA==" data-explain="V2VpZ2h0cyBjb3JyZWN0IHRoZSBlc3RpbWF0ZS4gQ2x1c3RlcmluZyBhZmZlY3RzIHRoZSB2 YXJpYW5jZTogaWdub3JpbmcgaXQgZ2l2ZXMgYSBzdGFuZGFyZCBlcnJvciB0aGF0IGlzIHRv byBzbWFsbC4="} Why must the PSUs be declared in svydesign() and not only the weights? - Adults in the same PSU are alike, and the standard error has to reflect that - The PSU removes the bias of the estimate, while the weights fix its variance - Weights alone cannot be used when the outcome is a yes or no variable - The software needs the PSU to find which adults answered the questionnaire ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="6cwpp2.vyudl6" data-show="VGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBhZHVsdHMgaW4gdGhlIHRhcmdldCBwb3B1bGF0aW9u" data-explain="RWFjaCB3ZWlnaHQgaXMgdGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBhZHVsdHMgYSByZXNwb25kZW50IHJlcHJl c2VudHMsIHNvIHRoZSB3ZWlnaHRzIGFkZCB1cCB0byBhbiBlc3RpbWF0ZSBvZiB0aGUgcG9w dWxhdGlvbiBzaXplLg=="} The weights of the 1,853 respondents sum to about 414,000. What does this number estimate? - The number of adults who were sampled before nonresponse - The number of PSUs that were chosen within the strata - The number of adults in the target population - The number of respondents with a complete questionnaire ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="6cx2xq.vyus2i" data-show="SWdub3JpbmcgdGhlIGRlc2lnbiBtYWtlcyB0aGUgcHJldmFsZW5jZSBsb29rIG1vcmUgcHJl Y2lzZSB0aGFuIGl0IGlz" data-explain="Q2x1c3RlcmluZyBhbmQgdW5lcXVhbCB3ZWlnaHRzIHJlZHVjZSB0aGUgaW5mb3JtYXRpb24g cGVyIHJlc3BvbmRlbnQsIHNvIHRoZSBwcm9wZXIgU0UgaXMgbGFyZ2VyIHRoYW4gdGhlIHNp bXBsZSByYW5kb20gc2FtcGxlIG9uZS4="} The naive SE of the prevalence is 0.0098 and the design-based SE is 0.0149. What does this show? - The design-based SE must be wrong, since it is larger than the simple one - Ignoring the design makes the prevalence look more precise than it is - The weights have corrected the bias but they cannot change the SE - The two SEs would be equal if the sample were big enough ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Surveys have **strata, clusters (PSUs) and unequal probabilities** - **Weight** = 1 / selection probability = adults represented - Unweighted estimates are **biased** when groups are over-sampled - `svydesign(ids, strata, weights, nest = TRUE)` once, then `svy*()` - The naive SE is **too small** ::: **Next:** Session 2: descriptive estimates

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
